To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

saturated fat intake is not associated with risk for cardiovascular disease, and that the replacement of saturated fats with carbohydrates is associated with an increased risk for cardiovascular disease.

1) the replacement of saturated fat intake with carbohydrates is not associated with a lower incidence of IHD, 2) the replacement of carbohydrates with saturated fat is not associated with an increased risk of IHD; and 3) the replacement of high GI value carbohydrates with low GI value carbohydrate is associated with a lower risk of IHD.

the risk of coronary heart disease (CHD) increases when high glycemic carbohydrates (HGC) replace saturated fatty acids (SFA) in the diet, whereas low glycemic carbohydrates (LGC) are not associated with increased risk of CHD.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between diet, nutrition and health.
the effects of replacing dietary saturated fat with carbohydrates.
how dietary fats and carbohydrates influence the risk of coronary artery disease (CAD).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
saturated fats are not harmful and that high GIvalue carbohydrates are harmful.
replacing saturated fats with refined carbohydrates increases risk of MI, whereas replacement of saturated fats with low GI carbohydrates may be beneficial.
saturated fat intake is not associated with increased risk of IHD.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the quality of carbohydrate is more important than quantity, and that refined carbohydrates, which are rapidly digested, absorbed, and metabolized, have physiologic consequences that are very different from those of unrefined carbohydrates.
the effect of carbohydrates on the risk of cardiovascular disease is not as simple as the effect of fats, and that carbohydrates should not be viewed as a single entity.
saturated fat is not bad and carbohydrates are not good.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the quality of carbohydrate is an important determinant of IHD risk and that replacing saturated fat with high quality carbohydrates is beneficial, whereas replacing saturated fat with low quality carbohydrates is not beneficial.
the GI of the carbohydrate source is a more important determinant of cardiovascular risk than is the carbohydrate content per se (1, 7).
the quality of carbohydrates is as important as the quantity in determining cardiovascular risk, as well as risk of diabetes.
